title: Unapproved Local Windows Firewall Rule Changes
exclusions: Detects locally added, modified, or deleted Windows Defender Firewall rules represented by Security events 4946, 4947, and 4948 when no exact, in-window approval exists for the host, action, normalized rule name, and changed profile. Microsoft explicitly states that these events are not generated for rule changes made through Group Policy. They do not report the initiating user, command, process, executable, protocol, address, port, old value, new value, whether the rule is enabled, whether traffic exposure changed, or whether the action succeeded maliciously. This detector does not cover firewall profile enable/disable changes, service impairment, WFP provider/callout/filter changes, IPsec rules, GPO/MDM policy changes, direct registry edits that emit none of these events, non-Windows firewalls, or packet allow/drop behavior. An unapproved row means governance did not match the observed local change; it is not by itself proof of compromise or ATT&CK behavior. This documentation review did not validate Windows auditing, collection, lookup governance, SPL, or alerting in production.
evidence: Retain the covered-host inventory; effective `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` policy; local-rule-merge policy; raw 4946/4947/4948 XML; `windows_firewall_rule_change_approvals.csv` revision and approval records; periodic `Get-NetFirewallRule -PolicyStore PersistentStore` and `ActiveStore` inventories where authorized; saved search `windows_unapproved_local_firewall_rule_changes` definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; source-health and audit-policy-health reports; alert actions; incident dispositions; and dated positive, approved, expired, wrong-key, GPO, duplicate-route, missing-field, and late-arrival tests. Each result preserves host, event and index time, event code/action, rule ID/name, changed profile, provider/channel, event record ID, approval state, lookup revision, raw event reference, and analyst conclusion. Documentation review generated no runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing Security event 4946 with `Computer=fw-lab-01`, `EventRecordID=9001`, `ProfileChanged=Public`, `RuleId={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, and `RuleName=Temporary Remote Admin`; provide no matching approval row. Expect exactly one row with `action=rule_added`, normalized `sample_host=fw-lab-01`, `profile_changed=public`, `approval_state=unapproved`, and the same rule/event identity. Repeat with 4947 and 4948 fixtures and expect `rule_modified` and `rule_deleted` respectively.
controlTest.negativeScenario: For the 4946 fixture, add an exact normalized lookup row for `fw-lab-01,rule_added,temporary remote admin,public` whose inclusive start is at or before event time and exclusive end is after it, with nonempty change ID, owner, approver, and lookup revision; expect zero alert rows while retaining the approved base event separately. Also expect zero rows for event 2004 from the Firewall Operational channel, event 4954, a 4946 event from the wrong provider/channel, a record missing RuleId or RuleName, and the same record received twice. An expired, future, wrong-host, wrong-action, wrong-name, or wrong-profile approval must still produce one unapproved row.

dataSources: Primary source: Windows Security log provider `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, event 4946 (local firewall rule added), 4947 (local rule modified), and 4948 (local rule deleted), collected in XML or classic rendering with Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742). Enable the Success setting for the Advanced Audit Policy subcategory `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` and verify effective policy on each covered host. Microsoft documents event version 0 fields `ProfileChanged`, `RuleId`, and `RuleName`; also retain host/computer, provider, channel, EventRecordID/RecordNumber, event time, and index time. Governance source: an exact, normalized, time-bounded approval lookup containing host, action, rule name, profile, start/end epochs, change ID, owner, approver, and revision. Optional inventory uses NetSecurity `Get-NetFirewallRule` against `PersistentStore` and `ActiveStore`; it is corroborating state, not an event field.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for Security event collection and extraction. A deployment-owned Windows firewall security app must provide audit-policy/source health, exact change-approval governance, inventory snapshots, saved search, fixtures, dashboard, and response runbook.
spl:
index=windows source IN ("WinEventLog:Security","XmlWinEventLog:Security") sourcetype IN ("WinEventLog","XmlWinEventLog") EventCode IN (4946,4947,4948) earliest=-15m@m latest=@m
| eval sample_host=lower(coalesce(Computer,dest,host)), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber), rule_id=lower(trim(coalesce(RuleId,RuleID))), rule_name=lower(trim(RuleName)), profile_changed=lower(replace(trim(ProfileChanged),"\\s+","")), provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName)
| where provider="Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing" AND len(sample_host)>0 AND len(event_record_id)>0 AND len(rule_id)>0 AND len(rule_name)>0 AND len(profile_changed)>0
| eval action=case(EventCode=4946,"rule_added",EventCode=4947,"rule_modified",EventCode=4948,"rule_deleted")
| dedup sample_host source event_record_id
| lookup windows_firewall_rule_change_approvals.csv sample_host action rule_name profile_changed OUTPUTNEW approved_start_epoch approved_end_epoch change_id change_owner approver approval_revision
| eval approval_complete=if(len(change_id)>0 AND len(change_owner)>0 AND len(approver)>0 AND len(approval_revision)>0 AND isnotnull(tonumber(approved_start_epoch)) AND isnotnull(tonumber(approved_end_epoch)),1,0), approval_state=if(approval_complete=1 AND _time>=tonumber(approved_start_epoch) AND _time<tonumber(approved_end_epoch),"approved","unapproved")
| where approval_state="unapproved"
| table _time _indextime sample_host EventCode action rule_id rule_name profile_changed provider source sourcetype event_record_id approval_state change_id change_owner approver approval_revision
| sort 0 - _time sample_host event_record_id
description: Reports one event-grain row for each complete, deduplicated Windows Security event 4946, 4947, or 4948 that records a local firewall rule add, modify, or delete and lacks an exact valid approval for the normalized host, action, rule name, and changed profile at event time. It reports an unapproved local rule-change record, not the actor, changed ports, effective exposure, or malicious outcome.
value: Promptly reconciling local firewall rule changes with approved work helps teams find unauthorized exceptions, accidental deletion of protective rules, unmanaged installer behavior, and possible defense impairment before the altered host policy enables unwanted connectivity. The preserved rule and event identity also gives responders a defensible starting point for inventory comparison and process investigation. This reduces the time that an unauthorized or dangerously broad local firewall exception can remain active.
implementation: Enable and verify Success auditing for `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change`, collect the Security channel through `Splunk_TA_windows`, and prove 4946–4948 fields on every supported Windows/rendering combination. Publish a normalized, exact, time-bounded change-approval lookup and separate audit/source-health searches. Save the SPL as `windows_unapproved_local_firewall_rule_changes`, run every five minutes over a measured 15-minute arrival window, and route each unapproved result to firewall/security owners for raw-event, current-policy, change, and process review. Do not infer actor or port exposure from these events.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — Local Firewall Rule Governance`: put covered hosts missing Security telemetry or effective MPSSVC auditing first; then show unapproved changes by action, host, profile, rule name, owner, and time, an add/modify/delete timeline, approval-match rate, late/duplicate records, and incident disposition. Drill down to raw 4946–4948 XML, exact approval row/revision, `PersistentStore` and `ActiveStore` inventory comparison, nearby process/PowerShell/registry/EDR evidence, and ticket. Label rows “unapproved local rule-change events,” never “firewall disabled,” “port opened,” or “attacker” without independent evidence.
schema: Windows Security Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change event schema plus deployment-governed exact change approvals
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary detector. Generic Change/All_Changes summaries do not guarantee preservation of event 4946–4948 RuleId, RuleName, ProfileChanged, event-record identity, local-versus-GPO semantics, or exact approval interval. A deployment may normalize a secondary Change event only after proving raw-event parity; accelerated Change counts cannot recover the absent actor, old/new rule body, or effective network exposure.

knownFalsePositives:
An unapproved result means the exact governance lookup did not match at event time; many legitimate local workflows can still cause it.

1. **Application installation, upgrade, or removal** — A signed installer may create, modify, or delete a local exception for its service. Verify package/product version, deployment job, signer/hash, endpoint-management record, exact rule name/ID/profile, installed rule body, and owner approval.

2. **Endpoint-management or configuration-management remediation** — Intune, Configuration Manager, DSC, Group Policy scripts, or another agent can write the local PersistentStore even when the business policy is centrally managed. Confirm agent process/job, policy assignment, local-versus-domain policy store, expected before/after inventory, ticket, and deployment ring. Do not assume every centrally initiated action is a GPO event omission.

3. **Administrator troubleshooting or emergency access** — Support staff may temporarily add a remote-management rule. Require incident/change ID, named host, exact rule/action/profile, start and exclusive expiry, accountable owner/approver, current inventory, and documented removal verification.

4. **Security, vulnerability, or compliance tooling** — A scanner, EDR, isolation workflow, or firewall posture tool can alter local rules. Verify product/version, signed process, policy/job ID, intended rule, vendor documentation, and whether the rule protects or expands access.

5. **Windows feature or service provisioning** — Enabling a role, optional feature, sharing, remote administration, or application capability can create predefined local rules. Validate feature-change event/package, service owner, rule group and current body, expected profiles, and approved baseline.

6. **Lab, red-team, purple-team, or control test** — Authorized tests intentionally create and remove rules. Require exercise ID, isolated approved systems, exact names/actions/profiles, fixed times, named operators, expected network test, cleanup, and retained evidence.

7. **Approval-key normalization or governance drift** — Host aliases, localized/display-name changes, spaces in ProfileChanged, stale lookup bundles, wrong epochs, or renamed rules can prevent a valid match. Compare raw XML, normalized values, lookup checksum/revision, search-head bundle, ticket, and UTC boundaries. Correct governance rather than broadly suppressing names.

8. **Duplicate forwarding or replay** — WEF plus local forwarding, queue replay, or cloned events can repeat one EventRecordID. The SPL deduplicates host/source/record ID inside the window; verify raw routes, channel record identity, collector subscription, and index-time delay before treating repeats as separate changes.

9. **Rule replacement represented as delete plus add** — An approved tool may replace a rule rather than modify it, producing two actions and possibly a new ID. Validate ordered events, exact old/new inventory, tool transaction, ticket scope, and resulting policy; never suppress all adds following deletes.

**Safe suppression:** populate `windows_firewall_rule_change_approvals.csv` before approved work with exact lowercase `sample_host,action,rule_name,profile_changed`, inclusive `approved_start_epoch`, exclusive `approved_end_epoch`, `change_id`, `change_owner`, `approver`, and immutable `approval_revision`. Reject wildcards, host groups, rule-name-only rows, blank profiles, open-ended windows, retroactive approval, and broad product/publisher exceptions. Apply approval after preserving the base event; keep approved results in a restricted review/evidence report. The lookup must not suppress audit-policy, source-health, missing-field, inventory-drift, or duplicate-route findings.
detectionType: TTP-aligned governed local firewall rule-change event
hardware: Supported Windows clients and servers running Windows Defender Firewall where local rule changes are permitted or relevant, `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change` Success auditing is effective, and Security events are centrally retained. Hosts governed exclusively through GPO/MDM need separate policy-change collection because Microsoft states 4946–4948 do not fire for Group Policy rule changes.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft MPSSVC audit-policy and Security event 4946/4947/4948 documentation, Windows Firewall policy-store guidance, current MITRE ATT&CK Windows Host Firewall semantics, and Splunk Microsoft Windows add-on documentation; auditing, source fields, approval lookup, SPL, fixtures, inventory correlation, alerting, dashboard, and response were specified but not executed or Windows/firewall/Splunk-SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: The base search scans three normally low-volume Security event IDs over 15 minutes, normalizes a few fields, deduplicates record identity, and performs one exact lookup. Cost scales with covered-host count, event duplication, and installer activity; source/event constraints should remain in the base term.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and claim boundary

Assign Windows firewall, endpoint engineering, change management, security operations, Splunk data/content, and incident owners. Inventory covered hosts, stable host identity, OS/build, firewall management authority, allowed local-policy-merge state per Domain/Private/Public profile, effective audit policy, Security channel capacity/retention, forwarder/WEC routes, add-on version, index/RBAC, approval owner, and decommission time.

Use the event contract precisely. Microsoft documents 4946 for a rule locally added, 4947 for a rule modified, and 4948 for a rule deleted. Their event version 0 payload consists of ProfileChanged, RuleId, and RuleName. Microsoft also says these events do not generate for changes through Group Policy. They carry no Subject block, user, process, command line, old/new rule body, application, protocol, address, or port. Therefore the detector reports an unapproved local rule-change event only. It cannot establish who changed the rule, whether an allow or block condition changed, or whether exposure increased.

Current MITRE ATT&CK maps adversarial Windows host firewall changes to T1686.003. A row is TTP-aligned because its behavior is one component of that sub-technique, but ordinary administration emits the same events. Do not title an alert “attacker disabled firewall” without independent policy, process, and network evidence.

## Step 1 — Configure and prove Windows auditing

Through domain policy, MDM, or an accountable local baseline, enable Success auditing for Advanced Audit Policy Configuration > Policy Change > `Audit MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change`. Verify effective state on every supported OS/build with `auditpol /get /subcategory:"MPSSVC Rule-Level Policy Change"` or the localized/equivalent management interface. Record policy source, precedence, and timestamp. Do not confuse this with `Audit Filtering Platform Policy Change`, Filtering Platform Connection, or packet-drop auditing; those produce different event families and answer different questions.

Size and monitor the Security channel so bursts are not overwritten before collection. Protect audit policy and log service configuration. Build `windows_firewall_audit_policy_health` to compare covered-host inventory with recent policy attestations and expected 494x source heartbeat/control tests. Silence is not proof that rules did not change. A missing event can mean auditing was disabled, collection failed, the operation came from GPO, or no local action occurred.

Document local rule merge policy. Microsoft explains that AllowLocalPolicyMerge can prevent locally authored rules from combining with centrally deployed policy on selected profiles. A local change event can still matter as attempted/configuration drift even if the rule is not effective in ActiveStore; separately determine the resultant policy.

## Step 2 — Collect and verify the Security event schema

Use Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742). In governed `inputs.conf` or WEC collection, enable the Security channel on covered hosts and route it to deployment-local `index=windows`; that index name is a documented local convention, not a Splunk default. Qualify both tested renderings: `source=WinEventLog:Security,sourcetype=WinEventLog` and `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security,sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Narrow production to forms actually deployed after field tests.

On a disposable lab host, add, modify, and remove one uniquely named local firewall rule using supported Windows tools. Export raw XML and verify provider `Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing`, channel Security, EventCode 4946/4947/4948, event version, ProfileChanged, RuleId, RuleName, Computer/host, EventRecordID or RecordNumber, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Confirm field capitalization for both classic and XML rendering. `RuleId` and `RuleID` are coalesced only to accommodate proven extraction spelling; do not invent a missing identifier.

Run a GPO-created rule test and record the expected absence of 4946–4948, consistent with Microsoft documentation. Validate GPO change collection separately through directory/GPO audit and policy inventory. Also test localized rule names and multiple profiles; the SPL removes whitespace from ProfileChanged but otherwise retains its comma-separated semantics.

Create `windows_firewall_rule_change_source_health` to report covered hosts without Security ingestion, wrong source/sourcetype, unexpected provider, missing payload fields, record-ID reuse, WEC/local duplicate routes, event-time/index-time delay, and parsing changes after add-on/Windows upgrades. Do not let an approval exception hide health failures.

## Step 3 — Govern exact approvals and inventory

Publish `windows_firewall_rule_change_approvals.csv` from the change system, not analyst memory. Normalize lowercase host, action (`rule_added|rule_modified|rule_deleted`), exact rule display name, and profile string without spaces. Include inclusive approved start epoch, exclusive approved end epoch, unique change ID, owner, approver, immutable revision, reason, and creation time. Validate start < end, bounded duration, no wildcards, complete ownership, unique keys/windows, UTC conversion, and approval predating execution.

Rule names are display strings and can be localized or duplicated. The Security payload's RuleId is retained for investigation but not used as the pre-change approval key because a newly created rule identifier may not exist when a request is approved. For modify/delete work, record expected RuleId in the ticket and verify it after matching; deployments with a reliable preauthorized ID may extend the lookup and SPL to require it. Never approve only `host=*`, `rule_name=*`, product publisher, or a long maintenance month.

Take periodic signed/restricted inventories with `Get-NetFirewallRule -PolicyStore PersistentStore` for local static policy and `Get-NetFirewallRule -PolicyStore ActiveStore` for the resultant set of all applicable stores. Microsoft documents that the default is PersistentStore and ActiveStore is the sum of policy stores. Capture Name/InstanceID, DisplayName, Enabled, Direction, Action, Profile, PolicyStoreSource/Type, owner, time, and associated address/port/application/service filters using the corresponding NetSecurity filter cmdlets. Inventory is state sampled at collection time, not proof of actor or exact transition.

## Step 4 — Create and understand the saved search

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_unapproved_local_firewall_rule_changes`. Schedule every five minutes with `earliest=-15m@m latest=@m` only after measuring p99 forwarding/index delay; set a longer measured window if WEC/forwarder queues require it. Use a durable checkpoint or notable suppression keyed on sample_host, source, event_record_id, action, and event time so overlapping windows do not repage while late events remain detectable.

The base term fixes the local index, Security source/rendering, and three event IDs. The first eval normalizes host; coalesces record and rule-ID extraction spellings; lowercases rule identifiers/names; removes profile whitespace; and preserves provider. The where clause rejects incomplete identity and any provider other than Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing. Action is derived solely from documented event code. `dedup sample_host source event_record_id` handles duplicate records within a dispatch, but cross-source duplicate collection remains a health defect requiring route correction.

The exact lookup joins normalized host, action, rule name, and profile. Approval is complete only with IDs/owners/revision and numeric epochs. Event time must be greater than or equal to start and strictly less than end. Only unapproved rows survive. Keep a companion audit report of approved matches with the same event identity; suppression is a notification decision, not deletion of evidence.

## Step 5 — CIM and adjacent evidence

Keep `cimModels=[]` for the primary contract. A local deployment can map the result to Change.All_Changes after detection, but the standard accelerated model is not evidence that every required raw payload and approval interval is retained. Do not replace the SPL with `tstats count by user,dest`: these events contain no user, and a count does not identify the firewall rule.

Collect Security 4688, Sysmon event 1, PowerShell 4104, EDR process telemetry, Windows Firewall Operational events, registry monitoring, service-control events, GPO/MDM audit, and firewall inventories only through separately tested contracts. Search nearby `netsh advfirewall`, `New/Set/Remove-NetFirewallRule`, management-agent, installer, Control Panel, registry, and service activity. Temporal proximity is not a causal join; require host/session/process evidence before naming an actor.

Compare PersistentStore and ActiveStore at or soon after event time. Retrieve associated port, address, application, and service filters because `Get-NetFirewallRule` does not embed all those details in the 494x event. Determine whether local merge is enabled and whether the changed rule is effective. Network flow, WFP allow/block, or controlled connectivity evidence is needed to establish exposure change.

## Step 6 — Validate logic, collection, and nonclaims

Build fixed-time fixtures for 4946, 4947, and 4948 with exact expected output. Test XML/classic rendering, RuleId/RuleID extraction, Computer/dest/host precedence, EventRecordID/RecordNumber, profile spaces, localization, casing, duplicate route, late arrival, null fields, wrong provider/channel/source/type, and events 2004/4950/4954. Assert one row per valid record and no fabricated actor or rule-body fields.

Test approvals at exact inclusive start, one second before exclusive end, exactly at exclusive end, expired/future windows, missing owner/revision, malformed epoch, wrong host/action/name/profile, duplicate lookup keys, stale bundle, and wildcard rejection. The end-boundary event must alert. Run approved and unapproved reports together to prove no event is lost.

On a disposable host, use a unique deny rule first to minimize exposure, then perform add, modify, and delete actions and compare Event Viewer, Splunk, PersistentStore, ActiveStore, and ticket. Do not open an inbound production port merely to create evidence. Run a separately approved GPO rule change to prove the documented blind spot rather than treating no event as detector success.

Load-test installer bursts, WEC fan-in, lookup bundle size, overlap, late events, scheduler concurrency, Security log overwrite, and retained raw volume. Verify RBAC permits analysts to see result identity while limiting sensitive raw/process evidence appropriately.

## Step 7 — Alert, investigate, and respond

Alert title: `Unapproved local Windows firewall rule <action> on <host>`. Include UTC event/index time, host, code/action, rule ID/name, profile, provider/channel/source, event record ID, approval state/revision, audit/source health, local-merge posture, inventory link, owner, and raw-event link.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw XML, provider/channel/code, record identity, normalized values, time/index delay, and duplicate route.
2. Re-run the exact approval match and inspect lookup revision, epochs, ticket, owner, and approver; distinguish absent approval from normalization failure.
3. Query current and retained PersistentStore/ActiveStore state, associated filters, policy source, profile, Enabled/Direction/Action, addresses, ports, application/service, and local-merge effect.
4. Identify the management method and probable initiator through process, PowerShell, EDR, installer, management-agent, registry, session, and change evidence; do not derive an actor from 494x.
5. Determine whether GPO/MDM or local policy should control this host and whether the resulting rule changes reachable traffic.
6. Review nearby authentication, remote-service, network, malware, persistence, and defense-impairment evidence for malicious context.
7. If unauthorized and risky, follow accountable endpoint/network incident procedure to contain access, preserve evidence, and restore an approved firewall baseline.
8. Confirm effective policy, intended connectivity, source/audit health, ticket closure, and no continuing changes before disposition.

Never automatically delete a rule, disable a service, isolate a host, block an account, or overwrite policy from one 4946–4948 row. A protective deny rule could have been added, or a dangerous allow rule deleted. Preserve current and prior state before remediation and coordinate changes that could interrupt production or management access.

## Step 8 — Troubleshooting and maintenance

- **No events after local test:** verify effective MPSSVC Success audit policy, Security channel, truly local PersistentStore action, provider/channel, WEC subscription/input, forwarder queues, source/type, index/RBAC, and event overwrite.
- **GPO change absent:** expected for 4946–4948 per Microsoft; use directory/GPO/MDM audit and resultant-policy inventory.
- **Rule fields null:** inspect raw XML and rendering/add-on extraction; confirm event version/provider. Do not substitute Message parsing without tests.
- **Too many installer results:** integrate exact package changes into bounded approvals; never suppress all adds or a vendor name indefinitely.
- **Approval does not match:** compare normalized lowercase host/name/profile, comma/space formatting, action, UTC epochs, bundle checksum, and duplicate rows.
- **Actor requested:** explain the payload limitation and correlate separately tested process/session evidence; never label system process IDs from the Event System block as the modifying user.
- **Rule body requested:** collect NetSecurity state/filter inventory; 4946–4948 do not contain ports, addresses, direction, action, program, service, or before/after values.
- **CIM count differs:** expected if normalization scope differs; raw Security identity is authoritative for this detector.

Review coverage inventory, audit policy, local merge, Security retention, source/rendering/fields, event-delay window, exact approvals, inventory collection, ATT&CK version, CIM decision, adjacent correlation, dashboard, RBAC, runbook, and exceptions quarterly and after Windows, firewall policy, GPO/MDM, WEC/forwarder, add-on, lookup, or Splunk changes. Keep `status=draft` until Windows firewall, endpoint, change, and Splunk owners execute and sign the validation matrix.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for firewall rules being added, changed, or removed directly on a Windows computer without a matching approved change. The record does not tell us who did it or which port changed, so the team checks the rule and other logs before deciding whether it was dangerous.
